newsitem.title: UK: UK industry eyes Labour's friendship. Will it last?.
newsitem.headline: UK industry eyes Labour's friendship. Will it last?.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government has sent shivers down the spines of some businessmen with an attack on the bonuses given to National Lottery executives and on the profits of privatised rail network operator, Railtrack.

Business pages in Britain's main newspapers condemned the government for sending the wrong signal to business and long-standing critics of Labour leaped on the announcement, saying they showed the new government was taking a gamble.
"I think the government is taking a risk actually by behaving in this particular way," Ruth Lea, head of the policy unit at the Institute of Directors, told Reuters.
But other business groups were more cautious, with the Confederation of British Industry declining to comment.

Others dismissed the attacks on Railtrack and lottery operator Camelot as special cases. The government was still enjoying a favourable response from business, which Labour courted assiduously during campaigning for the May 1 election which brought Labour to power, they said.
"I don't think they have put many feet wrong," David Botterill, chief executive of the Engineering Employers Federation for the West Midlands, told Reuters.

Most eyes remain fixed on Labour's first budget on July 2 -- in particular on whether there will be any changes in corporate taxes -- seeing it as decisive to relations between the energetic new administration and industry.
The two new rows both focus on private monopolies created by the former Conservative government, whose 18 year rule ended with Labour's landslide election victory.
Railtrack was set up to run the rail network and sold off as part of the Conservative privatisation drive.
Even before the election Labour, which long ago abandoned plans to buy back the privatised rail companies on cost grounds, criticised Railtrack for not meeting its investment obligations.

John Swift, the head of the rail industry regulator, Ofrail, has continued to criticise the company -- whose revenue mainly comes from track access charges levied on train operators -- for failing to plough enough of its profits back in investment.

Deputy prime minister John Prescott increased pressure on the company on Thursday by criticising Railtrack's announcement of 346 million pounds ($564.7 million) in pre-tax profit in its first set of annual results since privatisation.
"I've made clear I don't think that's a good deal for the taxpayer. I'm looking at how I can improve the taxpayer's interest in that matter," Prescott said.
The other row was over executive bonuses at Camelot.
After pressure from Heritage Secretary Chris Smith, the directors of the lottery operator said on Friday they would make payments from their bonuses to charity.

The government declared the matter closed, ending a row sparked by the announcement of the bonuses of as much as 176,000 pounds for top directors of Camelot in a year in which money raised by the lottery for good causes was falling.

But it came against a background of Labour's commitment to hand the lottery over to a non-profit making operator at the end of Camelot's franchise and a long campaign against huge payouts to "fat cat" directors of newly privatised utilities.
Financial Times columnist Philip Stephens attacked the new government for "sanctimonious posturing", saying it was not up to ministers but to shareholders to oversee executive pay.

Lea added: "What worries me generally is the kneejerk reaction to risk and profit... There are still people in government who haven't come to terms with a creation called business and business makes profit or goes bust."
But Botterill said: "I don't think the business community will be getting excited about either of these situations."
Business leaders had generally welcomed a range of moves made by Labour, he said, including the decision to give the Bank of England autonomy over interest rates.

The decisions to give back control over competitiveness to the department of trade and industry and to drop plans to change merger policy were also welcomed, as was the appointment of a string of top business people to advise the government.

But all those questioned agreed the defining moment in Labour's links to business had not yet come, although the budget -- in which Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will unveil his windfall tax on privatised utilities -- would be a key test.

"The moves so far have been very good, sound and sensible," said Botterill. "Where the crunch might come is when we see something of the colour of the budget; what is going to happen on the tax front to relieve the rise in interest rates." ($1=.6127 Pound)
